questions.knowledge_point: Solving a Quadratic Equation When the Solutions Are Irrational
questions.problem: The equation ${x}^{2}+4x-7=0$ can be written in the form $(x+p)^{2}=q.$   Find $p+q.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we move the constant term to the right-hand side and complete the square on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+4x-7 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}+4x & =7 \\ {x}^{2}+2\cdot 2\cdot x & =7 \\ {x}^{2}+2\cdot 2\cdot x+{2}^{2}-{2}^{2} & =7 \\ (x+2)^{2}-4 & =7\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we isolate the perfect square:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+2)^{2}-4 & =7 \\ (x+2)^{2} & =11\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $p=2,$ $q=11,$ and $p+q=13.$

questions.knowledge_point: Solving a Quadratic Equation When the Solutions Are Rational
questions.problem: The equation ${x}^{2}-2x+1=1$ can be written in the form $(x+p)^{2}=q.$ Find $\,pq\,,$ and the sum of the roots ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we move the constant term to the right-hand side and complete the square on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-2x+1 & =1 \\ {x}^{2}-2x & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-2\cdot x\cdot 1+{1}^{2}-{1}^{2} & =0 \\ (x-1)^{2}-{1}^{2} & =0 \\ (x-1)^{2} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $p=-1$ and $q=1.$ Thus, $pq=-1.$

We now solve the equation using the square root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-1)^{2} & =1 \\ \sqrt{(x-1)^{2}} & =\sqrt{1} \\ |x-1| & =1 \\ x-1 & =\pm 1 \\ x & =1\pm 1\end{aligned}
$$

We simplify the two solutions:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =1-1=0 \\ {x}_{2} & =1+1=2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the sum is ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=2.$

questions.knowledge_point: Solving a Quadratic Equation When the Solutions Are Rational
questions.problem: The equation ${x}^{2}-4x+4=1$ can be written in the form $(x+p)^{2}=q.$ Find $\,p-q,$ and the sum of the roots ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we complete the square on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-4x+4 & =1 \\ {x}^{2}-2\cdot x\cdot 2+{2}^{2} & =1 \\ (x-2)^{2} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

So, $p=-2,q=1,$ and $p-q=-3.$

Now, we solve the equation using the square-root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-2)^{2} & =1 \\ \sqrt{(x-2)^{2}} & =\sqrt{1} \\ x-2 & =\pm 1 \\ x & =2\pm 1\end{aligned}
$$

We simplify the two solutions:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =2+1=3 \\ {x}_{2} & =2-1=1\end{aligned}
$$

So, the solutions are ${x}_{1}=3$ and ${x}_{2}=1.$ Thus, the sum is $4.$

questions.problem: The equation ${y}^{2}+16=-12y$ can be written in the form $(y+p)^{2}=q.$ Find $p+q.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we move the constant term to the right-hand side, the $-12y$ term to the left-hand side, and complete the square on the left-hand side.

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}+16 & =-12y \\ {y}^{2}+12y & =-16 \\ {y}^{2}+2\cdot 6\cdot y & =-16 \\ {y}^{2}+2\cdot 6\cdot y+{6}^{2}-{6}^{2} & =-16 \\ (y+6)^{2}-{6}^{2} & =-16\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we isolate the perfect square:

$$
\begin{aligned}(y+6)^{2}-{6}^{2} & =-16 \\ (y+6)^{2} & =20\end{aligned}
$$

So, $p=6,q=20,$ and $p+q=26.$
